titre: DNA evidence first settled a family dispute
accroche: Leicester, 1984: a geneticist stumbles on a way to read DNA like a signature. His first case, in 1985, is not a crime.
contenu_vulgarise:
On September 10, 1984, at the University of Leicester, geneticist Alec Jeffreys is studying an X-ray film from a laboratory experiment on the DNA of one family, that of a technician on his team. The pattern he sees has nothing to do with what he was looking for: some portions resemble each other from one family member to the next, others differ entirely, in a way that is both inherited and unique to each individual. Within half an hour, Jeffreys understands that he holds a way to identify a person, and to trace kinship, from DNA alone. He names the method DNA fingerprinting.

## A paternity case, not a criminal trial

The first case where the technique is used involves neither murder nor theft. In 1985, a lawyer turns to Jeffreys for an immigration case: a family from Ghana, settled and naturalized in the United Kingdom, has a son who went back to Ghana and is refused entry on his return, his passport judged forged. With the father absent and the mother having several sisters in Ghana, the lawyer asks Jeffreys to check that the boy is indeed this mother's son, and not her nephew. Standard blood tests, which compare only a limited number of markers, had been unable to settle anything.

Jeffreys compares the disputed boy's DNA with that of the mother and her three other children, whose parentage is not in question. The result is clear: the mother and the boy are indeed related, and the four children share the same father. The British Home Office drops the case and the boy is admitted to the United Kingdom, to be with his family. Jeffreys later describes the relief visible on the mother's face when the result was announced. The scientific paper reporting the case, co-written with John Brookfield and Robert Semeonoff, appears in the journal *Nature* in late October 1985 under the title *Positive identification of an immigration test-case using human DNA fingerprints*.

## An order that matters

The technique thus first serves to reunite a family, before serving to unmask a culprit or clear a convicted man: which Jeffreys will do in 1986 and 1987, in the investigation of two murders committed near Narborough, not far from Leicester. This order is no mere anecdote: it shows that before being an instrument of criminal evidence, DNA fingerprinting was first an instrument of evidence in general, able to answer the most ordinary question there is, who is whose parent, with a reliability no earlier method came close to. The Leicester laboratory would remain, until the process was commercialized in 1987, the only one in the world able to carry it out.

repere.texte: In 1985, the DNA fingerprinting developed by Alec Jeffreys is used for the first time in a legal case: not a criminal trial, but an immigration dispute, where it establishes that a British boy was indeed his mother's son.
repere.source: Jeffreys, Brookfield, Semeonoff, “Positive identification of an immigration test-case using human DNA fingerprints,” Nature, vol. 317, pp. 818-819

carte.punch: DNA evidence first reunited a family, before unmasking a culprit
carte.idee: In 1984, Alec Jeffreys stumbles on DNA fingerprinting while studying the DNA of a family in his laboratory. Its first application, in 1985, is not a crime: it proves that a British boy is indeed his mother's son, in an immigration dispute.

quiz.question: What is the first case in which Alec Jeffreys applies his discovery of DNA fingerprinting, in 1985?
choix: The investigation of the Narborough murders, leading to the conviction of Colin Pitchfork
An immigration dispute, where it establishes that a boy is indeed his mother's son
A theft trial where it unmasks a suspect through traces left at a crime scene
A paternity test ordered by a French civil court in an inheritance case
quiz.explication: The technique's first application, in 1985, concerns an immigration case: it proves that a British boy of Ghanaian origin is indeed his mother's son, after standard blood tests had been unable to settle anything. Criminal cases, like Narborough, come afterward.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does Alec Jeffreys discover the principle of DNA fingerprinting on September 10, 1984?
choix: By deliberately comparing the DNA of several suspects in an ongoing police investigation
By studying an X-ray film from an experiment on the DNA of a technician's family
By reading an article by an American colleague who had already described the method without testing it
By receiving a commission from the British government to develop an identity test
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The discovery happens by chance: while examining an X-ray film from an experiment on the DNA of a technician's family in his laboratory, Jeffreys observes a pattern that is both shared among family members and unique to each of them.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where and when does the scientific paper reporting the first legal use of DNA fingerprinting appear?
choix: In the journal Nature, in late October 1985, signed by Jeffreys, Brookfield and Semeonoff
In an internal report of the British Home Office, kept confidential until 2003
In a British daily newspaper, which publishes the article before any scientific review
In a law journal, as a commentary on the immigration decision handed down
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The paper “Positive identification of an immigration test-case using human DNA fingerprints” appears in Nature (vol. 317, pp. 818-819) in late October 1985, co-signed by Alec Jeffreys, John Brookfield and Robert Semeonoff.
